Amillennialists respond that the passage's full realization is the consummated new creation, not pre-Parousia history; dispensationalists object that Christ's personal presence on the Mount of Olives (14:4) precedes the universal reign.

A future event at Christ's return, which inaugurates his millennial reign over the nations; the details may be literal or a mixture of literal and symbolic, but the sequence of coming, victory and a reign with remaining disobedience fits Revelation 19–20.
Like dispensationalists, historic premillennialists find 14:16–19 hard to fit into either the present age or the eternal state.
Amillennialists say the passage portrays one final victory, not two stages; partial preterists see 14:1–2 as AD 70.
Wheat and Tares, Mustard Seed and Leaven

Jesus gives three kingdom parables: an enemy sows weeds (zizania, probably darnel) among wheat, and the owner lets both grow until the harvest, when the weeds are burned and the wheat gathered (13:24–30, explained in 13:36–43 as the judgment at 'the end of the age', synteleia tou aiōnos); a mustard seed, smallest of seeds, becomes a tree in which birds nest (13:31–32); and a little leaven works through three measures of flour until all is leavened (13:33).

What do the parables teach about the kingdom between the two comings: steady growth to world-wide influence, a mixed field with good and evil coexisting until the end, or a 'mystery form' of the kingdom that includes corruption? And is 'the end of the age' the final judgment or the end of the Jewish age in AD 70?

The mustard seed and leaven promise that Christ's kingdom, though tiny in its beginnings, will grow extensively (filling the world, Daniel 2:35) and intensively (permeating every sphere of life) through the gospel before the harvest at Christ's return. The wheat and tares show the kingdom advancing in a world where evil persists until the end, but not that evil keeps pace with it.
Leaven works 'until all was leavened' (13:33), a picture of total permeation; birds nesting in branches echoes Daniel 4:12 and Ezekiel 17:23, where nations find shelter under a great kingdom.

Amillennialists answer that the parables stress the contrast of small beginning and large ending, not a timetable or a dominant majority in history; dispensationalists say leaven is consistently a symbol of evil (Matthew 16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Postmillennialists reply that context, not a fixed code, decides a symbol's meaning, and Jesus says the kingdom itself is like leaven.

The kingdom is truly present and growing through the church age, but it grows in a world where the enemy's sowing continues side by side until the harvest; the age ends with a single judgment separating righteous and wicked. No pre-consummation golden age is promised: the kingdom's triumph is real but hidden, and its full manifestation awaits Christ's return.

Wheat and weeds grow together 'until the harvest' (13:30), and the harvest is 'the end of the age' with one judgment of both groups (13:40–43), leaving no room for a millennium in between or a near-total eradication of evil before the end.

Postmillennialists say that 'coexistence' does not exclude 'proportion': the wheat can vastly outnumber the weeds. Premillennialists say a single harvest scene does not rule out an intervening kingdom phase revealed elsewhere (Revelation 20).

These parables describe the 'mystery form' of the kingdom during the interadvent age, after Israel's rejection of the King and before the millennial kingdom. Classic dispensationalists (e.g. Scofield, Pentecost) read the abnormally large mustard plant with birds (compare 13:4, 19, where birds are the evil one) and the leaven as pictures of corruption entering Christendom, so the age ends in apostasy rather than global conversion.

Jesus speaks of 'the mysteries of the kingdom' (13:11), suggesting something previously unrevealed; elsewhere in Matthew leaven means false teaching (16:6, 12), and the birds in this same chapter are agents of Satan.

Critics note that 13:33 says 'the kingdom of heaven is like leaven', making leaven a positive figure for the kingdom itself; and a mustard 'tree' with nesting birds echoes positive Old Testament imagery of nations finding shelter. Some progressive dispensationalists accept this and read the parables as growth parables.

Ladd's 'mystery of the kingdom': God's reign has entered history in a hidden, unexpected form, working secretly like seed and leaven without overpowering evil; it will be manifested in power at the Parousia, followed by the millennium and the age to come.
Explains why the kingdom foretold in Daniel 2 came first as a small, resistible presence rather than a world-crushing stone, and keeps both present reality and future consummation.
Postmillennialists say Ladd underplays the growth and final world-filling scope of the images; amillennialists see no need for the millennium Ladd adds after the harvest.

Partial preterists divide. Many (e.g. Gentry) read the harvest at 'the end of the age' as the final judgment; others (e.g. DeMar) note that synteleia tou aiōnos echoes the disciples' question in 24:3 and can denote the close of the old covenant age in AD 70, with the growth parables describing the kingdom's spread after that decisive judgment.
Matthew uses the same phrase in 24:3, which many link to the temple's destruction; Hebrews 9:26 places Christ's appearing 'at the end of the ages'.

Critics reply that 13:41–43 involves angels removing all lawbreakers and the righteous shining in the Father's kingdom, which fits final judgment better than AD 70; this is why many partial preterists, and all creedal readers, keep it future.

The harvest at the end of the age was the AD 70 judgment ending the Mosaic age, when the 'sons of the kingdom' who rejected Christ were cast out and the righteous shone in the established kingdom; the kingdom continues to grow after that point.
Holds 13:39–40 and 24:3 to the same 'end of the age', which Jesus placed within his generation (24:34).

This view denies a future final judgment at Christ's return, placing it outside historic creedal orthodoxy (Westminster Confession 33); critics also note the universal scope of 'all causes of sin and all lawbreakers' (13:41). Proponents answer that the creeds must yield to Scripture's time statements.
The Great Commission

The risen Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (echoing Daniel 7:14), commands the eleven to 'make disciples of all nations' (panta ta ethnē), baptizing and teaching them to observe all he commanded, and promises to be with them always, 'to the end of the age' (synteleia tou aiōnos).

Does the commission imply its own success, the discipling of nations as nations so that the world is largely Christianized before Christ returns, or does it command a faithful worldwide witness that gathers a people from every nation while the world remains mixed or worsens?

The commission rests on Christ's universal authority (Daniel 7:13–14 fulfilled at his resurrection and ascension) and therefore implies its own accomplishment: whole nations will be discipled, baptized and taught to obey Christ, with his presence guaranteeing the result. History will see the gospel's widespread triumph before 'the end of the age'.

The command is grounded in authority already possessed, not in a hoped-for future; 'make disciples of all nations' is more than 'preach to'; Psalm 2:8 and 22:27, Isaiah 2:2–4 and Daniel 2:35 promise global success.

Amillennialists answer that a command does not predict its degree of success, and Jesus elsewhere forecasts persecution and lawlessness (Matthew 24:9–12). Postmillennialists reply that these warnings refer largely to the pre-70 generation, and that Christ's authority makes defeat of the commission unthinkable.

The commission will certainly be fulfilled in the sense God intends: a people is gathered from every nation (Revelation 5:9; 7:9) and Christ is present with his church until the end of the age, his final return. It does not promise that a majority of the world will be converted; faithful witness under suffering continues alongside the growth of opposition.

'All nations' in Matthew typically means peoples from every nation (24:14; 25:32); the age ends with both wheat and weeds present (13:30); the New Testament expects tribulation for the church throughout the age (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).

Postmillennialists say this reduces Christ's universal authority to a remnant-gathering task; amillennialists answer that the gathering of a countless multitude from every tribe is no small victory and that God's sovereignty does not require statistical majorities.

The mandate of the church age is world evangelization and the calling out of a people for Christ's name (Acts 15:14), not the Christianization of nations. The age ends in apostasy and the Tribulation; the nations are judged and the kingdom established by Christ himself at his return (Matthew 25:31–46).
2 Timothy 3:1–5, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 and Luke 18:8 forecast decline; Christ, not the church, establishes the visible kingdom.

Postmillennialists object that this outlook reads the commission's grounding in Christ's present authority too lightly; amillennialists agree that the commission is evangelistic but deny a separate church-age parenthesis. Dispensationalists answer that Christ's authority is fully at work in gathering his church from all nations now, and will be displayed openly when he returns to reign.

The church proclaims the gospel to all nations as a witness (Matthew 24:14), a task that is itself a sign of the end and must be completed before Christ returns to establish his millennial reign; the kingdom's present power operates in mission, but its consummation awaits the Parousia.
Ladd stressed that the church's mission is the means by which God's reign advances now, giving missionary urgency without promising a Christianized world.
Postmillennialists say Ladd's 'witness' framing understates the command to disciple nations; amillennialists accept most of the reading but not the millennium.

Many full preterists hold that the universal-preaching benchmark (Matthew 24:14) was met before AD 70 (Colossians 1:6, 23; Romans 10:18), and that 'the end of the age' was the close of the Mosaic age at that time. Most still regard evangelism as an ongoing duty in the endless new covenant age; a minority question whether the commission as such binds the church today.
Paul's statements that the gospel had gone to 'all creation under heaven' (Colossians 1:23) are taken as signalling that the end of 24:14 arrived in that generation.

Critics argue that the promise 'I am with you always' and the command to disciple all nations hardly expired in AD 70, and that Paul's language is hyperbolic or representative; full preterism's denial of a future Second Coming also places it outside the historic creeds.
Before You Finish the Cities of Israel

Sending the Twelve on mission, Jesus warns of persecution and says that when they are persecuted in one town they should flee to the next, for they 'will not have gone through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes'.

What 'coming' of the Son of Man fits a timeframe shorter than completing a mission to Israel's towns? Albert Schweitzer made the verse the cornerstone of his view that Jesus mistakenly expected the end during the disciples' first tour.

The coming is Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70: the disciples' mission to Israel would not be completed before the Son of Man came, as Daniel 7 foretold, to vindicate himself and end the old order. The persecution described (synagogue floggings, governors and kings, 10:17–18) fits the apostolic generation in Acts.
The time limit is real and short; 10:17–22 reaches beyond the first tour to the whole period of apostolic witness; Matthew 16:28 and 24:34 place a 'coming' within the generation.

Critics ask why a 'coming' in Roman armies is called the Son of Man's coming; preterists answer that the Old Testament speaks of the LORD 'coming on the clouds' in historical judgments (Isaiah 19:1). Others argue the mission to Israel was hardly 'not completed' by AD 70 in any meaningful sense.

The verse refers to the one Parousia of Christ, which occurred in AD 70 within the lifetime of those addressed. Russell and later preterists cite it as evidence that the New Testament expected one coming only, in that generation.
Matthew elsewhere uses 'the coming of the Son of Man' for the Parousia (24:27, 37, 39); the time limit is strict.

Denying a future bodily return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy; critics also note that the New Testament describes the Second Coming as visible and universal (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

Many Reformed interpreters see a 'coming' in the vindication events that follow the cross: Jesus's resurrection and enthronement (28:18), the gift of the Spirit, and the judgment of AD 70 as stages of the one coming of the Son of Man to receive the kingdom, which is consummated at his final return.
Ridderbos's 'fulfilment in stages' explains why the Gospels attach both near and far time markers to the Son of Man's coming; Matthew 26:64 says 'from now on' the Son of Man will be seen.
Some say this multiplies 'comings' to escape a difficulty; others ask why the same phrase means different events in nearby texts.

The coming is the Second Coming: the mission of Christ's followers to the Jewish people will continue, amid persecution, and will not be completed before the Son of Man returns. On this reading the verse is a promise of continuing mission to Israel, not a deadline.

10:17–22 broadens beyond the first tour to the whole age; Matthew's other uses of 'the Son of Man comes' point to the Parousia; Carson argues the saying assures continued opportunity in Israel until the end.
The word 'finish' (teleō) sounds like a time limit on a task, not open-ended continuation; preterists see this as reading in a long delay.

Many dispensationalists read the mission to Israel as interrupted by Israel's rejection of the King and resumed during the future Tribulation by Jewish witnesses (Revelation 7:1–8), who will not finish going through Israel's towns before Christ returns. Others favour a near reference to Jesus rejoining the disciples after their mission.
The kingdom offer was to Israel first (10:5–6); the persecution described in 10:17–22 resembles Tribulation conditions in Matthew 24:9–14.
Critics object that the instructions were given to the Twelve in their own day, and that a gap of millennia in the middle of a single paragraph is hard to justify.
Some Standing Here Will Not Taste Death

After calling disciples to take up the cross, Jesus says the Son of Man will come in his Father's glory with his angels and repay each person according to what he has done (16:27), and then that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (16:28). Mark 9:1 and Luke 9:27 speak of seeing 'the kingdom of God' (Mark: 'come with power'); all three Gospels place the Transfiguration immediately after.
What did 'some' of the bystanders see before dying, and is verse 27 the same coming as verse 28?

Verse 28 refers to Christ's coming in judgment and kingdom vindication in AD 70, which 'some', not all, of the disciples lived to see. Many partial preterists (e.g. Gentry) distinguish verse 27, the final judgment of every person, from verse 28; others (e.g. DeMar) read both verses of AD 70, with 27 describing covenantal judgment on that generation.
'Some will not taste death' implies a span long enough that most bystanders would die, which suits roughly forty years better than six days; the wording matches 24:30–34 and 26:64.

Critics note that the Synoptic placement before the Transfiguration, and Peter's own appeal to the Transfiguration as eyewitness of Christ's 'power and coming' (2 Peter 1:16–18), point to a nearer fulfilment.

Verses 27 and 28 describe one event: the Son of Man came in glory with his angels, rendered judgment to each, and established his kingdom in AD 70, within the lifetime of some hearers. Because the repayment of 'each person' was then, the final judgment is past.
The 'for' (gar) linking the verses and the unbroken flow from glory, angels and judgment to 'some standing here' are taken to forbid splitting them.

Treating the judgment of 'each person' as past places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy; critics also argue that 16:27 echoes the universal judgment of Psalm 62:12 and Romans 2:6. Proponents answer that the creeds cannot outrank Jesus's time limit.

The Transfiguration, six days later, is a preview and pledge of the Son of Man's kingdom glory, seen by Peter, James and John; it begins a series (resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, and arguably AD 70) by which Jesus's kingdom 'comes with power', all anticipating the final coming of 16:27.

All three Synoptics attach the saying directly to the Transfiguration; Mark's version ('the kingdom of God come with power') fits Pentecost and the resurrection; 2 Peter 1:16–18 calls the Transfiguration a witness of Christ's 'power and coming'.

Preterists object that 'some will not taste death' is a strange way to describe an event six days away when none had died; amillennialists answer that the expression stresses privilege and certainty rather than delay.

The Transfiguration is a preview of Christ's future millennial kingdom glory: Peter, James and John saw in miniature the King coming in his kingdom, while 16:27 refers to the future Second Coming and judgment.
2 Peter 1:16–18 explicitly connects the Transfiguration to Christ's 'coming'; the immediate narrative sequence; Moses and Elijah suggest the kingdom with glorified and living saints.
Critics note the plural 'some' and 'not taste death' suggest a longer interval, and partial preterists argue the Transfiguration was a vision of glory, not a 'coming in his kingdom'.

The kingdom 'come with power' (Mark 9:1) refers to manifestations of God's reign within the disciples' lifetime, beginning with the Transfiguration and resurrection and especially Pentecost; the Parousia of 16:27 remains future and inaugurates the millennium.
Ladd's already/not-yet: the kingdom is God's dynamic reign, which can 'come with power' before its consummation.
Preterists say this fails to explain the 'Son of Man coming' wording in Matthew; others see it as merging distinct events.
An Hour Is Coming When All in the Tombs Will Hear

Jesus says the hour is coming and now is when the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and live (5:25), then adds that an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (5:28–29), echoing Daniel 12:2.

Does 'an hour' teach a single general resurrection of righteous and wicked together, ruling out a thousand-year gap between two resurrections (Revelation 20:4–6)? And is the resurrection of 5:28–29 bodily and future, or fulfilled spiritually or corporately?

One general resurrection of all people, righteous and wicked, at Christ's return, followed by one final judgment. The 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:5 is the believer's present spiritual life with Christ or the soul's entrance into heaven, as 5:25 describes a present spiritual resurrection followed in 5:28–29 by a future bodily one.

Both groups rise in the same 'hour' at the same voice; Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15 likewise speak of one resurrection 'of both the just and the unjust'; John 6:39–54 places believers' resurrection on 'the last day'.

Premillennialists reply that John's own 'hour' in 5:25 has already lasted two thousand years, so an 'hour' can span a millennium. Amillennialists answer that 5:25 is a spiritual hour by its nature, whereas 5:28–29 concerns a single bodily event at the last day.

Agrees with the amillennial reading: one bodily general resurrection and judgment at Christ's single return after the millennial period of gospel prosperity; 5:25 describes the spiritual resurrection by which the kingdom grows now.
The two-stage pattern (spiritual resurrection now, bodily resurrection at the end) is how Augustine and the Reformed confessions understood Revelation 20 and John 5.
Premillennialists raise the same 'hour' objection; full preterists say the bodily-future reading ignores the near-coming context of John's eschatology.

Jesus speaks of the resurrection of both groups without specifying whether they occur together; as 'the hour' of 5:25 spans the whole church age, the 'hour' of 5:28 can contain both the resurrection of the righteous at Christ's return and the resurrection of the rest after the thousand years (Revelation 20:5).
Revelation 20:4–6 explicitly separates a first resurrection of the blessed from 'the rest of the dead'; 1 Corinthians 15:23–24 lists an order ('each in his own order').
Amillennialists respond that John's Gospel consistently places the righteous's resurrection 'on the last day' (6:39–54), leaving no later day for the wicked to be raised.

There are distinct resurrections in sequence: of the church at the rapture, of Old Testament and Tribulation saints at Christ's return, and of the wicked after the millennium (Revelation 20:5, 11–15). John 5:28–29 describes the two kinds of resurrection, not their timing.
Revelation 20 gives a thousand-year gap; 'the resurrection of life' and 'the resurrection of judgment' are qualitatively distinct, like the 'better resurrection' of Hebrews 11:35.
Critics say this multiplies resurrections beyond the text and conflicts with the single 'hour' and single 'last day' of John's Gospel.

The resurrection of 5:28–29 occurred in AD 70, when the dead were raised from Hades (the realm of the dead) into God's presence and the judgment took place; it was not the reanimation of physical corpses. Some, following Max King, see a corporate resurrection of the covenant people from the 'death' of the old covenant.
Ties 5:28–29 to Daniel 12:2, whose fulfilment Daniel 12:7 places at the shattering of the holy people's power, which proponents identify with AD 70.

Denying a future bodily resurrection places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy (Nicene and Apostles' Creeds); Wright and others argue that 'resurrection' in Jewish and Christian usage meant bodily life after death, and 'all in the tombs' denotes bodies. Proponents answer that Hades-to-heaven language fulfils the text without physical bodies.
Will You Restore the Kingdom to Israel?

The disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He replies that it is not for them to know the times or seasons the Father has fixed, but they will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the end of the earth. He is taken up and a cloud hides him; two men in white say this same Jesus will come in the same way as they saw him go.

Does Jesus affirm a future restoration of national Israel (only the timing is withheld), or redirect the question so that the kingdom is restored through the Spirit-empowered witness to the nations? And what does 'in the same way' imply about the manner of his return?

Jesus does not correct the disciples' expectation of a restored kingdom for Israel; he corrects only their curiosity about timing. The kingdom will be restored to Israel at his return, which will be personal, bodily and visible to the Mount of Olives (1:11–12; Zechariah 14:4), after the present church age of witness.

After forty days of teaching about the kingdom (1:3), the apostles' question is assumed to be informed, not confused; 'times or seasons' implies there is a time; Acts 3:21 and Luke 22:29–30 keep Israel's restoration in view.

Covenant theologians respond that Jesus's answer replaces the national-political horizon with a universal one (1:8), and that the Spirit's coming, which the prophets tied to Israel's restoration (Isaiah 32:15; 49:6), is the beginning of that restoration.

Jesus redirects the question: Israel's restoration is being accomplished now as the Spirit is poured out and the witness goes from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, fulfilling Isaiah 49:6, where restoring Jacob and being a light to the nations are one task. The return 'in the same way' is Christ's personal, visible Second Coming at the end of the age.
Acts 1:8 echoes Isaiah 49:6 and 32:15; Acts 15:16–18 interprets the rebuilt tent of David as the inclusion of Gentiles; the gathered remnant of Jews in Acts 2 is the restored Israel's nucleus.

Dispensationalists respond that this reads Isaiah selectively and that Jesus's answer would be misleading if the disciples' premise was wrong; amillennialists answer that Jesus regularly reframed questions (e.g. John 3:4).

The witness 'to the end of the earth' is the program by which Christ's kingdom expands until it fills the world; his return 'in the same way' is the final, bodily, visible Second Coming after that expansion. Postmillennial partial preterists such as Gentry insist that Acts 1:11 is not the AD 70 coming but the future Parousia.
The parallel of ascension in a cloud and return in a cloud, the stress on 'this same Jesus', and the eyewitness emphasis ('as you saw him go') all point to a personal, visible return.

Amillennialists accept the bodily return but question the expected scale of success before it; full preterists object that the same 'cloud coming' language in the Gospels is applied to AD 70 by partial preterists themselves.

The return 'in the same way' means 'in a cloud', as the Old Testament describes the LORD coming in clouds of judgment; Christ returned in that manner in AD 70, discerned by faith rather than by physical sight. Restoration of the kingdom to Israel was the establishment of the new covenant people.
Consistency with the AD 70 interpretation of 'coming on the clouds' in Matthew 24:30 and 26:64, which partial preterists themselves accept.

Critics argue that 'this same Jesus' and 'in the same way as you saw him go' stress a visible, bodily departure and return; denying a future bodily return places the view outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

The church's mission and the Spirit's coming begin the restoration hope, while the bodily return of Christ will establish his reign on earth for the millennium; whether ethnic Israel has a special place in that reign is debated within the tradition.
Keeps both the redirection of 1:8 and the literal return of 1:11, without requiring a pretribulational framework.
Dispensationalists see too little emphasis on Israel; amillennialists see no need for a millennium between the return and the new creation.
Times of Refreshing and the Restoration of All Things

Peter calls the people of Jerusalem to repent so that their sins may be blotted out, 'times of refreshing' may come from the Lord's presence, and he may send the Christ appointed for them, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things (apokatastasis pantōn) spoken of by the prophets.

Is the 'restoration of all things' a millennial restoration of Israel's kingdom triggered by national repentance, the progressive subduing of Christ's enemies while he reigns from heaven, or the final new creation at his return?

Peter re-offers the kingdom to Israel: if the nation repents, Messiah will return and bring the restoration the prophets foretold, the millennial kingdom with Israel at its centre. Israel's rejection postponed this, and the restoration awaits national repentance at the end of the Tribulation.

Acts 3:20 says Jesus was appointed 'for you' (Israel); 'restoration' echoes the disciples' question in Acts 1:6 (the verb apokathistēmi); the prophets' restoration oracles centre on Israel's land and kingdom.

Non-dispensationalists question whether the kingdom was 'offered' and 'postponed', and note that Peter immediately applies the promise to Abraham's blessing of 'all the families of the earth' (3:25–26).

The restoration of all things is the consummated new creation at Christ's return. Christ remains in heaven, reigning, until that day; when he comes, the restoration is complete. This leaves no room for an earthly millennial reign after his return before the final state.

'Heaven must receive him until' sets the Second Coming as the moment of restoration; Romans 8:19–23 and Revelation 21:5 ('I make all things new') describe the cosmic renewal the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 65:17).
Premillennialists respond that a millennium is the first stage of the restoration and the new creation its completion; postmillennialists stress that the restoration is in progress before the return.

Christ must stay in heaven until the restoration is accomplished: he rules from his throne now, subduing his enemies through the gospel (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25), and returns only when that work has run its course. The passage thus implies that the restoration is a historical process brought to completion before the Second Coming.
Psalm 110:1 ('sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool') and 1 Corinthians 15:24–26 together place the subduing of enemies during Christ's heavenly session, before his return.

Amillennialists answer that 'until the restoration' may mean 'until the time when restoration happens', at the return itself, not after a process; premillennialists say Psalm 110 does not specify the means of subjection.

The restoration begins at Christ's return with his reign over a renewed earth, the millennium, and is completed in the new heavens and new earth; repentance brings present 'refreshing' through the Spirit as a foretaste.

Coheres with Acts 1:6 and Romans 11's hope for Israel without the postponement theory; the prophets whose restoration Peter cites (3:21) picture a renewed earth with Israel and the nations at peace (Isaiah 11; 65), which premillennialists see beginning visibly at the return.
Amillennialists argue that the restoration of 'all things' at the return is total, not partial.

The restoration of all things was completed when the old covenant world passed and the new covenant order was fully established in AD 70; the 'times of refreshing' are the new covenant life now available in Christ.
